To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chickens infected by mosquito feeding had a higher viral dose than those inoculated by needle.

mosquito-infected chickens had viremic and viral shedding levels up to 1 000 times higher at early times post-infection than needle inoculated chickens, and that a high dose of WNV inoculated by needle was required for enhanced early infection.
mosquitoes inoculate chickens with a higher viral dose than needle inoculation with a similar dose and that the early infection is enhanced in chickens infected by multiple mosquito bites.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of mosquitoes and mosquito-borne viruses in the epidemiology of arboviral disease.
understanding how mosquito transmission of WNV affects viral infection in the host and how mosquito infection and feeding behavior may be manipulated to reduce transmission.
understanding the role that mosquito transmission of WNV plays in viral replication and pathogenesis in the vertebrate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the early viremia in chickens infected by mosquito bites is enhanced compared with those infected by needle inoculation and is due, at least in part, to a higher viral inoculum.
mosquito transmission of arbovirus results in enhanced early infection in the vertebrates.
the enhanced early infection in mosquitoes-infected chickens may not be solely explained by the high viral dose inoculated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mosquitoes transmit WNV at a higher dose and more efficiently than needles.
the mosquito bite is the best way to deliver the virus to a vertebrate host, because it delivers more virus and the virus is more likely to be delivered in the right place.
the mosquito bite inoculation method is a useful tool for studying early WNV infection and pathogenesis in chickens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mosquito transmission of WNV can lead to higher early infection in the host and that this may have implications for the course of WNV infections in vertebrates.
the early viremia in mosquito-infected birds is much higher than in needle-inoculated birds, which may be a key factor for the transmission of WNV by mosquitoes.
the route of infection may affect the course of WNV infection in chickens, which has implications for studies on WNV pathogenesis in the avian host.
